content: Anthelmintics are pharmacological agents designed to eliminate parasitic worms, also known as helminths, from the host organism. These drugs achieve their effect by either killing the parasites outright or paralyzing them, thereby facilitating their expulsion from the body. Traditional remedies with similar effects are often referred to as vermifuges (which expel worms) or vermicides (which kill worms). Classes of Anthelmintic Drugs and Their Efficacy: 1. Albendazole: This drug is effective against a wide range of helminths, including threadworms, roundworms, whipworms, tapeworms, and hookworms. 2. Diethylcarbamazine: It is specifically used to treat infections caused by Wuchereria bancrofti, Brugia malayi, Brugia timori, tropical pulmonary eosinophilia, and loiasis. 3. Mebendazole: This medication is effective against pinworms, roundworms, and hookworms. 4. Niclosamide: It is primarily used to treat tapeworm infections. 5. Ivermectin: This drug is effective against most common intestinal worms, with the exception of tapeworms. 6. Suramin: While not specified in detail, it is another anthelmintic agent. 7. Thiabendazole: It is effective against roundworms and hookworms. 8. Pyrantel pamoate: This drug is used to treat most nematode infections. 9. Levamisole: Another anthelmintic agent, though specific targets are not detailed here. 10. Praziquantel: It is effective against nematodes and certain trematodes. 11. Triclabendazole: This drug is specifically effective against liver flukes. 12. Octadepsipeptides (e.g., Emodepside): These are effective against a variety of gastrointestinal helminths. Additionally, many drugs within the piperazine family have proven to be effective anthelmintics. Natural Anthelmintics: Certain natural substances are also known to have anthelmintic properties. These include black walnut, wormwood (Artemisia absinthium), clove (Syzygium aromaticum), tansy tea (Tanacetum vulgare), Hagenia (Hagenia abyssinica), kalonji (Nigella sativa) seeds, and the male fern (Dryopteris filix-mas). In Brazilian folk medicine, plants such as Plumeria acutifolia or Plumeria rubra are also used as anthelmintics. However, it is crucial to note that many natural anthelmintics can be toxic to humans if used improperly or in incorrect dosages, posing significant risks alongside their effects on parasites. Anthelmintic Resistance: Anthelmintic resistance refers to the ability of parasitic worms to survive treatments that are typically effective when administered at the recommended dose. This phenomenon is a growing concern and represents a significant threat to the effective control of worm parasites, particularly in small ruminants and horses. Mechanism of Resistance Development: When treatment is administered, worms with genotypes that make them susceptible to the drug are eliminated. Resistant worms, however, survive and pass on their resistance genes to subsequent generations. Over time, the population of resistant worms increases, leading to treatment failure. Clinically, resistance is defined as a reduction of less than 95% in the fecal egg count following treatment. Factors Contributing to Resistance: 1. Frequent Treatments: Administering treatments at frequent intervals, such as three or more times per year, accelerates the development of resistance. On some farms, treatments are given more than six times annually, further exacerbating the issue. 2. Treating All Animals Simultaneously: When all animals in a group are treated at the same time, there is no refugia (a population of untreated worms that can dilute the resistant population). This lack of refugia promotes the survival and propagation of resistant worms. 3. Treating and Moving to Clean Pastures: When animals are treated and then moved to clean pastures, there is no dilution of resistant worms by susceptible ones, further contributing to resistance. 4. Underdosing: Administering doses that are lower than the recommended amount allows worms with low-level resistance to survive and reproduce, gradually increasing the prevalence of resistance in the population. These factors collectively underscore the importance of strategic and judicious use of anthelmintics to mitigate the development of resistance and preserve the efficacy of these critical drugs.
